entry.question:
## Physical scenario

You are a research scientist working on a high-energy particle accelerator. Using a modern version of the Thomson \( e/m \) apparatus, you want to measure the mass of a muon (a fundamental particle that has the same charge as an electron but greater mass). The magnetic field between the two charged plates is \( 0.340\,\text{T} \). You measure the electric field for zero particle deflection as a function of the accelerating potential \( V \). This potential is large enough that you can assume the initial speed of the muons to be zero. An \( E^2 \)-versus-\( V \) graph of your data.

## Question

Use the graph to calculate the mass \( m \) of a muon.

## Answer choices

- A: A: 1.63 \times 10^{-28}\

- B: B: 1.85 \times 10^{-28}\

- C: C: 2.25 \times 10^{-28}\

- D: D: 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\

## Figure caption (auxiliary; use the image as primary evidence)

The image shows a graph with a linear relationship between two variables. The x-axis is labeled \(V \, (\text{V})\), representing voltage in volts, with intervals marked at 0, 100, 200, 300, and 400. The y-axis is labeled \(E^2 \, (10^8 \, \text{V}^2/\text{m}^2)\), representing the square of the electric field in units of \(10^8 \, \text{V}^2/\text{m}^2\), with intervals at 0, 200, 400, 600, and 800.

The graph has a series of black dots representing data points, which form a straight line, indicating a strong linear relationship. A magenta line connects the dots, emphasizing the linearity. The relationship suggests that as voltage increases, \(E^2\) increases proportionally. The grid lines in the background help to align and determine the values of the data points.
